performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
question: How does imitation turn separate orchestral groups into a collective finale?
intro: A horn call releases fast string motion; dance, sustained melody and imitative counterpoint compete within the same finale. Follow what happens when a theme is passed between parts rather than simply repeated.

sections.label: Horn call
sections.mNote: the short Pesante summons precedes the continuous motion

sections.label: Fast string motion
sections.mNote: Presto figures spread from strings through the orchestra

sections.label: Contrasting span and build
sections.mNote: the texture thins before a substantial new accumulation

sections.label: Quiet imitative centre
sections.mNote: small entries accumulate into a contrapuntal argument

sections.label: Renewed orchestral drive
sections.mNote: a later high-pressure span gathers the instrumental groups

sections.label: Quiet plateau
sections.mNote: the Tranquillo region reduces weight before the long final build

cues.title: A call before the rush
cues.text: The horns open with a short, weighty call. The strings then set the fast motion in train: a change from a signal that can be answered to a current that must be sustained.
cues.evidence: Score p. 79, opening Pesante, acceleration and Presto at bar 8: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report begins relatively quietly and grows through the first half-minute. The 0:08 map anchor is score-proportioned, not an instrument-detection result.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Motion gathers a larger body
cues.text: The opening motion is no longer only a light string texture. Listen for the way its smaller figures retain their identity while the recorded sound gains weight and sharper articulation.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −25.9 dB at 0:10 to −12.3 at 0:30, with onset activity increasing around 0:35–0:45 and novelty at 0:38. Score pp. 79–85 supplies the expansion beyond the initial string texture: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf.

cues.title: The difficult last movement
cues.text: Writing to his son Péter in September 1943, Bartók said that four movements were complete but the last was proving especially difficult. The finale’s abundance should not be mistaken for effortless composition.
cues.evidence: The letter of 26 September 1943 is quoted with sources in Brett Van Gansbeke’s history: https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto . The cue does not attach the difficulty to one particular bar.

cues.title: A crest before a withdrawal
cues.text: The early fast span reaches a crest, then quickly loses weight. Hear that withdrawal as preparation for contrast, not as an attempt to bring the finale to an early conclusion.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-finale.txt: level near −11 dB at 1:45–1:50 falls to −21.8 at 1:55 and −29.9 at 2:00; novelty at 2:00. No cadence or thematic identity is inferred from the drop.

cues.title: A line against continuing motion
cues.text: Through the contrasting material, separate the foreground phrase from whatever continues beneath it. A longer line need not stop the motion of the accompaniment; two kinds of movement can coexist.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 97–104, thinner wind-led writing and the later sustained material over moving strings: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report locates a lower-level span after 2:00, but its onset detector cannot determine whether each accompaniment note is audible separately.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The new span accumulates force
cues.text: The quieter contrast grows into a substantial orchestral crest of its own. Follow the length of the increase, rather than expecting every new figure to restart the argument.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty at 2:46; level rises from −24.8 dB at 2:35 to −14.7 at 2:50 and −8.6 at 3:25. This supports the overall build, not a single uninterrupted crescendo mark.

cues.title: The Boston beginning
cues.text: Koussevitzky conducted the premiere with the Boston Symphony Orchestra on 1 December 1944. This Pittsburgh recording belongs to the work’s early reception, before it became a standard orchestral showpiece.
cues.evidence: Rodda’s Pittsburgh Symphony programme notes give the premiere in Boston Symphony Hall: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. The historical score’s erroneous Carnegie Hall statement is explicitly corrected in Móricz’s source description E: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf.

cues.title: Counterpoint at a smaller scale
cues.text: The quiet central passage rebuilds the music through imitation. Listen for a recognisable shape entering in another part while the earlier line continues, rather than for a melody accompanied by passive chords.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 110–113, Un poco meno mosso from bar 256 and successive entries: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report’s deep trough at 3:45 and renewed onset activity through 4:00–4:15 anchor this approximate imitative region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Following more than one line
cues.text: Choose one line for a few moments, then shift attention to another. Counterpoint changes what “foreground” means: the interest may lie in how the parts meet, not in one instrument always taking command.
cues.evidence: The interlocking parts are visible through the developmental score, pp. 111–123: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report confirms sustained activity in this broad region but does not isolate the voices; this is a listening exercise, not a timestamped entry claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A score corrected by Bartók
cues.text: Reiner’s conducting score survives with corrections made by Bartók himself. The critical edition identifies that manuscript copy as the performing source for the Pittsburgh recording, rather than assuming Reiner used an unaltered printed score.
cues.evidence: Móricz, Comments, sources CR and RecR; Reiner’s score is held at Northwestern University: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf. The stage map uses the available historical print only for broad orchestration, not every difference in that manuscript.

cues.title: Pressure followed by another retreat
cues.text: This later orchestral crest is followed by a surprisingly deep withdrawal. The finale reserves room for one more long approach instead of sustaining maximum force to the end.
cues.evidence: Report: high windows at 5:50 (−9.3 dB) and 6:05 (−9.7), followed by −25.7 at 6:15 and −28.5 at 6:20; novelty at 6:26. No beat speed is inferred from these levels.

cues.title: Quietness without immobility
cues.text: The quieter plateau still has motion inside it. Listen beneath the sustained line for accompaniment that keeps the music alive while its larger gestures become less forceful.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 128–136, Tranquillo from bar 449 and subsequent sustained wind writing over moving strings: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Quiet windows from 6:20 through 7:15 and novelty at 6:40/6:54 anchor the broad region. Low detected onset counts are not treated as proof of slow notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An ending revised before recording
cues.text: Bartók supplied a longer ending after the premiere. Reiner’s Pittsburgh recording uses that revision; the critical edition distinguishes it from Koussevitzky’s December 1944 broadcast, which preserved the original close.
cues.evidence: Móricz, sources A-endR, RecK and RecR: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf. The cue concerns the version of the whole finale, not a claim that the alternative ending begins at 7:12. The printed alternative starts at bar 602, score pp. 145–147: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf.

cues.title: A long final ascent
cues.text: The last large build gathers weight over an extended span. Compare its patience with the short initial horn call: the ending is earned by accumulation rather than by one sudden return of the opening signal.
cues.evidence: Report: level increases from −30.3 dB at 7:15 to −18.4 at 7:20, −14.0 at 7:45, −9.8 at 8:00 and the movement’s highest five-second window, −8.5 at 8:05. This describes a broad rise, allowing local fluctuations.

cues.title: After the largest crest
cues.text: The loudest stretch is not the final instant. Keep following the moving figures after that crest; the revised ending still has room to gather and release its own last burst.
cues.evidence: Highest level is around 8:05, followed by changing levels and renewed onset activity at 8:25–8:35. Score pp. 143–147 supplies the remaining closing material and expanded ending: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. No alternative-ending first bar is asserted at 8:24.

cues.title: The full orchestra closes
cues.text: The expanded ending gathers the orchestra for a final rising gesture and emphatic close. Let the remaining resonance distinguish the last attack from the end of the file.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 145–147, alternative ending through bar 625, with brass glissandi and percussion reinforcement: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report marks novelty at 8:50, renewed level at 8:55 and decay by 9:00; no sample-exact final attack is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The signal releases continuous motion
transitions.how: The short Pesante call leads through an acceleration into the Presto. The strings replace separated signals with continuous motion, while quieter sustained support holds the new texture together. This is a change of function as well as pace: the opening summons becomes an ongoing argument.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 79, bars 1–8 and following: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The 0:08 anchor is a score-proportioned estimate within the opening build; the report’s onset-tempo value is not used to identify Presto.

transitions.title: Motion thins to expose a line
transitions.how: The first sustained drive loses orchestral weight. A more exposed line can emerge against continuing motion, changing the listener’s focus without making the accompaniment inert. This thinner contrast will itself grow into a substantial crest.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 97 onward, thinning around bar 148 and subsequent wind-led passage: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 2:00 and the fall to −29.9 dB support this approximate contrast boundary.

transitions.title: A large crest gives way to small entries
transitions.how: The broad accumulation recedes and the Un poco meno mosso passage starts on a smaller scale. Harp and divided strings prepare an imitative texture in which one part can enter while another continues. The change replaces orchestral mass with the interest of interacting lines.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 110, bar 256 and successive entries on pp. 110–112: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 3:36 and 3:44, followed by the quietest window at 3:45. Passage alignment, not exact bar synchronisation.

transitions.title: Small exchanges gain collective weight
transitions.how: The violins retain their rapid figures while horns add a more sustained profile above the lower strings’ repeated pulses. Trumpets and trombones then strengthen the accented replies, and the string motion spreads again through the lower parts. The build enlarges the orchestral grouping without requiring all the parts to move in the same rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 122–127, especially bars 394–413 and following: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Report: novelty at 5:46, level −19.2 dB at 5:40 rising to −12.3 at 5:45 and −9.3 at 5:50. The scored layers describe the surrounding build; individual entries are not bar-synchronised.

transitions.title: The orchestral weight falls away again
transitions.how: The later drive retreats into the Tranquillo region. Longer lines and a lighter accompaniment reduce the sense of pressure while retaining motion underneath. The withdrawal reserves space for the final accumulation instead of spending the whole ending at maximum force.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 128 onward, Tranquillo from bar 449: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The low-level span around 6:20 and novelty at 6:26/6:40 support the approximate placement, not an exact tempo-change bar.

transitions.title: The quiet plateau starts to gather
transitions.how: The strings keep their flowing figures while longer wind and brass lines accumulate above them. Clarinet, low brass and cor anglais colours make successive contributions before the fuller later sound. Because the accompaniment never stops moving, the increasing weight can feel continuous even though no single instrument carries the entire rise.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 130–136, layered entries around bars 498–543: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Report: −30.3 dB at 7:15 followed by −18.4 at 7:20, then a long rise towards 8:05. The 7:16 anchor marks the broad start of that accumulation, not a precise new theme or chord.

transitions.title: The close receives additional room
transitions.how: Bartók’s alternative ending extends the closing argument beyond the shorter original version. Acceleration, renewed orchestral entries and the final rising gesture give the accumulated energy more room to resolve. Reiner uses this expanded ending, not the close heard in the first Koussevitzky broadcast.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 145–147, alternative ending from bar 602: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf; Móricz identifies the recorded version in source RecR: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf. The approximate 8:38 placement is proportioned within the closing span before novelty at 8:50; it is not a measured splice or exact first bar.

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, V, including alternative ending
source.locator: Printed pp. 79–147. The alternative ending on pp. 145–147 matches the version identified by Móricz for Reiner’s 1946 recording. Passage snapshots use measured contrasts and approximate score proportions, with roughly 10-second tolerance; not instrument recognition or a claim to reproduce every manuscript correction.

timeline.note: The horns give the opening Pesante call (p. 79).
Fast string motion emerges over quieter sustained support; the first violins join the second violins’ initial motion (pp. 79–80).
The opening drive expands through wind and brass participation around the mobile strings (pp. 81–90).
A thinner bassoon-led region contrasts with the preceding accumulation (p. 97 onward).
Sustained wind and brass material sits above continuing string figures, broadening towards a full crest (pp. 103–109).
Un poco meno mosso starts quietly with harps and divided violins before the imitative texture grows (p. 110).
Successive string lines and short wind phrases build the imitative centre; no one group remains sole leader (pp. 111–113).
The later drive gathers strings, winds and brass into a fuller orchestral span (pp. 123–127).
The Tranquillo region and its continuation set sustained wind lines over moving, often muted strings (pp. 128–136).
The long closing accumulation recruits greater wind and brass weight around the continuing string motion (pp. 135–144).
The revised ending adds a final orchestral rise, brass glissandi and side-drum/cymbal reinforcement (pp. 145–147).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
